description: We're recruiting people who've special inhuman powers to for a team for the 'REENTRY'.
summary:
Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map (Marswalk 3D) is a Mars EVA planner that plugs NASA data into an ultra-local single spacewalk view. Insert waypoints, identify hazard zones and the planner courses around hazards, calculates distance, EVA time for an 8 hour life support, radiation dose and a GO or Caution verdict. A solar particle event scenario reveals space-weather risk, a preloaded Gale Crater science loop illustrates it.

Imagery on the map incorporates Mars Trek Viking mosaic, MOLA topography, and THEMIS thermal infrared images. A 3D route view depicts terrain areas that AI has identified, with Curiosity REMS camera images and weather, and values from Mars Climate Database for pressure, density, wind, and dust.

Quantum Echo AI, modeled after the Mars Climate Database, forecasts surface, air temperature, and pressure across any location and time of sol, such as a surface temperature curve over the course of a day. It gives typical error, warnings within the trained range, and MOLA coverage indicating where it is reliable.

Marswalk 3D solves this by taking the challenge on - transforming these huge global datasets into a route plan for individual trips, now with safety as the priority. Why it matters: the first Martian explorers require reliable local information on cold, low-density air, dust, radiation, rugged terrain, and suit-time constraints.
details:
What is it and how does it work?

Marswalk 3D plans a Martian spacewalk. User selects a map of actual NASA images, drops waypoints, draws circular hazard areas, and the app navigates around each hazard on the shorter side. It computes distance, EVA time at either rover speed (10 km/hr) or on-foot speed (2.5 km/hr), plus 20 min science per stop, and compares with life-support 8-hr limit, and estimates radiation dose. Gives a GO or caution verdict with reasons. A toggle switches a space-weather-warning, simulating solar-particle event, and verdict is adjusted.

You can open the route in a 3D view rendered from MOLA elevation data, with hazards as walls, the route as a tube with a rover marker and terrain zones colored by pattern. Clicking anywhere in Analyse mode will give you all sorts of information - our Quantum Echo model (a scikit-learn model that simulates the Mars Climate Database) will tell you the surface and air temperature and pressure, for that point in space and that point of sol, and draw a full-day temperature curve. There's a FastAPI backend on top of both the model and terrain data, and a React app - and a separate API endpoint of pressure, density, wind and dust values directly from the real Mars Climate Database.

What can it do for me?

Mars Trek and others operate at regional and global scale, this is at one trek.
It layers optical, thermal, topographic, atmospheric and radiation context in one area, a data type requested in the challenge.
The AI prediction responds immediately rather than having to wait on a third-party service.
Any prediction has its typical error and a message showing whether it's outside its training range that lets crews know not to rely on it.

What is the intended impact?

It demonstrates how a wealth of mission data can be rolled into a decision tool for those first human explorers. These crews will need to make quick, local decisions based on fearsome cold, lack of oxygen, dust, radiation, challenging terrain and limited suit time. Everything takes second place to safety, so hazards, time limits and radiation dominate the outputs.

Which tools, programming languages and software have you used?

Frontend: JavaScript React 19, Vite, Leaflet (2d map), Three.js (3d views), CSS.
Backend: Python 3.11 or 3.12, FastAPI, uvicorn.
ML and data: scikit-learn 1.6.1 (Ridge regression and Extra Trees), NumPy, pandas, SciPy, joblib.
Testing: pytest, plus ESLint on the frontend.
NASA Mars Trek tiles (Viking, MOLA, THEMIS), the Mars Climate Database, Curiosity REMS weather and camera images, Curiosity RAD dose data.
Hardware: only Standard computers No special hardware.

In what way is it creative?

AI as a climate proxy: Quantum Echo learns the Mars Climate Database's responses from terrain and sun geometry so it can respond immediately for any location.
Terrain zones discovered by AI: the terrain grid is grouped, and the 3D view is filled with colours corresponding to the pattern. The elevation data become more meaningful to an astronaut.
Honest doubt: the app informs the user as to which number it's unsure of, instead of just spitting out a confident looking number.
Automatic detours: roads curve to go around dangers rather than merely warn about them.
Mission feel - console styling, a spinning globe, a Gale Crater preset and a history of 10 landing sites make it feel like mission software.

What factors did your team consider?

Space crew safety counts: time restrictions, risks, radiation and straight up beware beacons lead the decision.
The app says that the weather forecast is an estimate, the values in the climate database are from models at a 1 m height, and the radiation dose is one constant rate. The solar particle event is an example.
Missing data: low data warning is activated where there is insufficient MOLA coverage and the telemetry panel defaults to a labeled baseline if the live Curiosity stream is not available.
Reasonable assumptions: the speeds, stop times and 8-hour limit are explicit planning assumptions.
Reliability: Tests cover the model, features and API; and the app remains functional if the remote external climate data base is down.
Reproducibility: pinned library versions and a documented setup means anyone can run it.
